title: How Coyotes Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the coyote (Canis latrans): its place in the genus Canis, North American origins, size and appearance, diet and hunting, fission-fusion social structure, family and denning habits, litter size adjustments tied to population census howls, and its evolution alongside and after wolves. They cover the historical extermination campaigns (poisoning, shooting, government programs), the 1970s ban on poisons and Endangered Species Act protections, coyotes' spread into suburbs and cities such as Chicago and Atlanta, and modern coyote management, including hazing and keeping pets safe. They also discuss rare human attacks, coy-dogs and coy-wolves, coyotes in Native American mythology as tricksters, and a listener email about a Jacksonville murder case. Opening includes tour announcements and the episode ends with a listener mail segment and sign-off.

segments.title: Tour plugs and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts promote upcoming live shows and joke about pronunciation and band names, then discuss Canis genus, dog family origins, and coyotes being native to North America.

segments.title: Coyote basics and urban coyotes
segments.summary: Hosts discuss coyote scientific name, subspecies, their persistence, personal experiences seeing coyotes in neighborhoods, and that coyotes are adapting to become active at dawn and dusk near people rather than strictly diurnal or nocturnal.

segments.title: Appearance and early sightings
segments.summary: Coyotes are described as wolf-like with narrower snouts, bigger than foxes, and roughly two to five feet nose to tail. Lewis and Clark initially mistook one for a fox.

segments.title: Coyote diet and clever hunting
segments.summary: Coyotes eat mostly mammals but also fruit and insects. Stories describe coyotes climbing trees for fruit, jumping fences, digging under, and a cat saving a child from a coyote attack.

segments.title: Fission-fusion packs and lifespan
segments.summary: Coyotes shift between hunting alone and in packs depending on prey and resources. Lifespan in the wild is about six to eight years. Coyotes mate for life, and litter size can change based on population density, signaled by howl responses.

segments.title: Dens and family structure
segments.summary: Coyotes raise young in dens, often taking over and expanding another animal's den. Family units include alphas, betas, helpers, and slouches. Young may be driven out to find territory.

segments.title: Lone coyotes, rabies, and distemper
segments.summary: Lone coyotes are not necessarily rabid. Rabies among coyotes was largely eradicated through oral vaccine baiting, though distemper and rabies can still occur. Coyotes playing with dogs can transmit distemper; the black coyote Carmine was trapped after befriending a Great Pyrenees in Smyrna.

segments.title: Origins and evolution alongside wolves
segments.summary: Coyotes evolved in North America from earlier canids, possibly descended from red wolves. Early coyotes were larger but competed with wolves; coyotes shrank and filled the rabbit and rodent niche, and the more aggressive ones died out.

segments.title: Extermination campaigns and the Endangered Species Act
segments.summary: Ranchers' losses led to government programs that poisoned, shot, and trapped wolves and coyotes, with the Biological Survey developing poisons. Opposition grew and Nixon banned poisons in the 1970s; the Endangered Species Act gave coyotes protection from extinction. Coyotes expanded into new regions, including the Apostle Islands and cities like Chicago. Killing programs continue.

segments.title: Coyotes in cities and wolf extinction link
segments.summary: Coyotes thrive in urban areas where wolves cannot. Wolf extinction removed natural checks on coyote populations. Lethal control of coyotes has ripple effects that increase reproduction, and hosts discuss tolerating a known coyote versus a more aggressive replacement.

segments.title: Livestock losses and pet safety
segments.summary: Ranchers report losses of sheep, lambs, and chickens to coyotes; hosts advise keeping cats indoors and not leaving small dogs out unattended at dawn, dusk, or overnight.

segments.title: Coyote attacks on humans and hazing
segments.summary: Human attacks are rare. Two cases are described, a 1981 California child and a 2009 Canadian hiker death, with hypotheses about den season and wolf hybridization. Non-lethal hazing with noise and waving arms is recommended, and keeping small dogs on short leashes.

segments.title: Coy-dogs, dingoes, and mythology
segments.summary: Coy-dogs and coy-wolves are discussed, along with the idea of keeping coyotes as pets being a bad idea. Dingoes are mentioned. Coyotes were portrayed negatively after Mark Twain's writing but are a trickster figure in many Native American myths, especially Southwestern tribes.

segments.title: Listener mail: Jacksonville murder case
segments.summary: A listener writes about a 1998 Jacksonville, Florida case in which a 14-year-old neighbor killed an 8-year-old girl and hid her body under a waterbed. Hosts discuss the case and the listener's note.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and give the show's contact information.
